subject: Maths
scope: First school mock: AQA Year 1 Pure only, sections A–H and J; no Statistics, Mechanics, Year 2 functions, radians or calculus.
notes: 24 original compact recall/application checks, prioritising proof, 2D vectors and graph transformations, plus integer binomial expansion, inequalities, derivative and definite-integral interpretation. Does not certify all first-mock statements.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: For an arbitrary integer n, how can you show the product of two consecutive integers is even?
cards.back: n(n+1) is even because one of two consecutive integers is even.
accept: n(n+1) is even because one of two consecutive integers is even.
One of n and n+1 must be even, so their product is even.
Two consecutive numbers contain an even integer, making their product even.
reject: Checking only n=1 is proof for every integer.
Every pair of consecutive integers is odd.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: How can you show the sum of any two odd integers is even using algebra?
cards.back: Write them as 2m+1 and 2n+1; their sum is 2(m+n+1), an even integer.
accept: Write them as 2m+1 and 2n+1; their sum is 2(m+n+1), an even integer.
Let the odd numbers be 2m+1 and 2n+1; the sum is a multiple of two.
Their sum equals 2 times an integer.
reject: Two odd numbers always sum to another odd number.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: A statement applies only to integers n with 1 ≤ n ≤ 4. Which cases must proof by exhaustion check?
accept: All four cases one, two, three and four.
Check 1 through 4 inclusive.
reject: Checking n=1 and n=4 is always enough.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: What must a counterexample do to disprove an implication 'if P then Q'?
accept: Satisfy P but fail Q.
Make the assumption true and conclusion false.
Meet the condition P and contradict the claimed result Q.
reject: Only show a case where P is false.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: Given A = (−2, 5) and B = (4, 1), what is vector AB?
accept: B minus A gives 6 in x and minus 4 in y.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: What is the magnitude of the vector (−6, 8)?
accept: 10 units.
Square root of 36 plus 64, equal to ten.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: If a vector has a negative x-component and a positive y-component, in which quadrant does its direction lie?
accept: Quadrant II.
Second quadrant.
Quadrant 2.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: If AB = (4, 6) and AC = (6, 9), why are A, B and C collinear?
cards.back: AC = 1.5 AB, so the two displacement vectors are parallel and share A.
accept: AC = 1.5 AB, so the two displacement vectors are parallel and share A.
AC is three halves AB, with the same starting point A.
The vector from A to C is a scalar multiple of the vector from A to B.
reject: AB and AC have different magnitudes so cannot be collinear.
Equal slopes alone show the points form a triangle.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: A and B have position vectors (1, 6) and (7, −2). What is their midpoint's position vector?
accept: Average the x-coordinates and y-coordinates to obtain (4,2).

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: For a = (3, −1) and b = (2, 4), calculate 2a − b.
accept: Two a is (6,-2); subtract b to get (4,-6).

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: What happens to the point (2, 5) on y = f(x) after transforming the graph to y = f(2x)?
accept: It moves to (1, 5).
The x-coordinate halves, and y stays five.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: Under y = 3f(x), what happens to a point (2, −4) on y = f(x)?
accept: It maps to (2, −12).
The y-coordinate triples while x stays two.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: How does y = f(x + 4) − 2 transform y = f(x)?
accept: Translate 4 left and 2 down.
Left four units and down two units.
Translation vector (−4, −2).

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: If (3, −2) lies on y = f(x), what point lies on y = f(−x)?
accept: Reflect the x-coordinate in the y-axis; y stays minus two.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: If (−4, 3) lies on y = f(x), what point lies on y = −f(x)?
accept: Keep x as minus four, reverse the sign of y.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: For positive integer n, what is the coefficient of x² in (1 + 2x)⁴?
accept: Twenty-four.
4C2 times 2 squared equals 24.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: What is the value of 5C2 and what does it count?
cards.back: 10; the number of ways to choose two objects from five without order.
accept: 10; the number of ways to choose two objects from five without order.
Ten, the number of unordered pairs from five objects.
Five choose two equals ten.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: For a geometric progression, what happens to the sign of successive terms if the common ratio is negative?
cards.back: Their signs alternate, provided the starting term is non-zero.
accept: Their signs alternate, provided the starting term is non-zero.
Successive nonzero terms alternate positive and negative.
Multiplying by a negative ratio switches the sign at each step.
reject: Every term must have the same sign.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: When solving (x+1)/(x−2) > 0, which value must always be excluded from the solution?
cards.back: x = 2, because it makes the denominator zero.
accept: x = 2, because it makes the denominator zero.
Two is excluded because the expression is undefined.
Never include x equals two.
reject: x = −1 because the denominator is zero there.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: A tangent has gradient −2. What is the gradient of the normal at that point?
accept: Positive one half; the gradients multiply to minus one.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: If f′(a) = 0 and f″(a) = 0, does the second derivative test alone tell you whether there is a maximum or minimum?
accept: No; the test is inconclusive.
No, another argument is needed.
Second derivative equal to zero cannot by itself classify the point.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: If a curve is below the x-axis between two roots, how does that section contribute to total geometric area?
cards.back: Use the positive magnitude of its definite integral.
accept: Use the positive magnitude of its definite integral.
Take the absolute value of that signed integral.
Negate the negative signed integral to count the area positively.
reject: Include it as a negative area in the total geometric area.
Ignore the section below the x-axis.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: Two non-vertical lines have gradients 3/4 and −4/3. What is their relationship?
cards.back: They are perpendicular because their gradients multiply to −1.
accept: They are perpendicular because their gradients multiply to −1.
Perpendicular; the product of their slopes equals minus one.
They meet at a right angle.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.front: For 0° ≤ θ < 360°, why must solving sin θ = 1/2 usually produce two solutions?
cards.back: Sine is positive in quadrants I and II, giving 30° and 150°.
accept: Sine is positive in quadrants I and II, giving 30° and 150°.
The solutions are 30 degrees and 150 degrees.
Positive sine gives a first-quadrant and a second-quadrant angle.
